questions.question: What two properties are required in the increasing-sequence version of the Monotone Convergence Theorem?
options: The sequence is decreasing and has no lower bound, no matter which values are selected.
The sequence is monotonically increasing and has a finite upper bound
The sequence is finite and has a maximum term
The sequence is unbounded and increasing

questions.question: For an increasing sequence satisfying the Monotone Convergence Theorem, what is its limit equal to?
options: The finite upper bound $M$ in every case

questions.question: Suppose $(a_n)$ is increasing and $a_n\leq 10$ for all $n$. What does the Monotone Convergence Theorem guarantee?
Which sequence is increasing with an upper bound $3$?
Why is boundedness essential in the Monotone Convergence Theorem?
options: Boundedness forces every sequence to be decreasing
Boundedness removes the need for a limit concept
Monotonicity alone does not prevent divergence
Monotonicity and boundedness are unrelated to convergence

questions.question: What is the corresponding statement for a decreasing sequence mentioned?
options: A decreasing sequence with an upper bound always diverges
A decreasing sequence with a lower bound converges to its infimum
A decreasing sequence converges to its supremum in every case
A decreasing sequence must become constant

questions.question: Let $(a_n)$ be increasing, $a_n\leq 5$ for all $n$, and let $s = \sup\limits_{n\ \geq 1}a_n$. What conclusion follows?
For $a_n=1-\dfrac{1}{n}$ with $n\geq1$, why does the monotone convergence theorem apply?
options: It is increasing and unbounded, so the theorem gives no finite limit
It is increasing and bounded above, so the theorem guarantees convergence
It is decreasing and has no lower bound
It is not a sequence of real numbers

questions.question: Which statement is a common overclaim beyond the Monotone Convergence Theorem?
options: Every bounded monotone sequence is convergent
An increasing sequence with a finite upper bound is convergent
The limit of an increasing bounded sequence is its supremum

questions.question: Why does the Monotone Convergence Theorem use $\sup\limits_{n\ \geq 1}a_n$ rather than simply the largest term?
options: An increasing bounded sequence may approach a non-term value.
The supremum is always the first term
The largest term always exists for infinite sequences
The supremum is unrelated to upper bounds

What does the increasing version of the Monotone Convergence Theorem conclude?
For an increasing bounded sequence, what set determines the limit in the Monotone Convergence Theorem?
options: Only the upper bound $M$ in every case
The set of all sequence values $\{a_n:n\ge1\}$

questions.question: What two ideas are combined in the Monotone Convergence Theorem?
If $(a_n)$ is increasing and $a_n\le 8$ for all $n$, what does the Monotone Convergence Theorem guarantee?
If $(a_n)$ is increasing and $\sup_{n\ge1}a_n=6$, what is its limit?
Which sequence fits the increasing-and-bounded-above pattern?
Why does an increasing sequence with no finite upper bound fall outside the stated increasing version?
options: The theorem assumes the sequence is decreasing.
The theorem assumes a finite upper bound.
The theorem applies only to finite sequences.
The theorem requires the first term to be zero.
